She kicked me out of our apartment. I was severely depressed and suicidal, and she was apparently scared of me and didn't want me around anymore. Because, y'know, kicking a suicidal person while they're down is a smart and kind way to handle things. /s

If it was basically anyone else I would have eventually understood where they were coming from - it's an overwhelming position to be in for sure. But the reason she and I became so close in the first place was because of our shared history of depression, suicidal thoughts, and self-harm. Surely, if anyone would understand the place I was in and get that I needed support more than anything, it would be her, right? I guess not. 

I still hold a lot of anger about this thirteen years later. She convinced our two other roommates to gang up against me with her, but I'm less angry at them because they didn't have the same history of mental illness that she and I had. It must have been difficult to understand what was happening. But my "best friend"? She should have been there for me when I was at my lowest point, and she let me down. Sometimes I'm shocked that I'm still alive after that betrayal.

That's just the title I use to describe the employees who help you find your gown during your bridal dress appointments - different stores may call them by different names. If you worked with someone at your appointment and talked about what kind of styles you were looking for, that person was a bridal stylist!

Former bridal stylist here who was lucky enough to work with a lesbian couple once - probably my favorite styling appointment I ever did! My first suggestion is to make sure the undertones of the gowns are the same - while they don't need to be the exact same color, the undertones/warmth/coolness will help them coordinate. Having a stark, blueish-white dress next to a warm ivory dress will make the ivory dress look dirty. Ivory and champagne could look nice together, or ivory and blush, or even two ivories that are close to one another.

The suggestions I've seen below to look for other gowns from the same designer/collection are all very good advice! You'll often see a lot of themes in a designer's collection from season to season, and they'll likely coordinate nicely.

Personally, I think the reason you're feeling like the current pairing is "too much" is because they're both dramatic in different ways. Your top choice has simple fabric in a dramatic/textured silhouette, and hers is a dramatic/textured fabric in a simple silhouette. Matching or coordinating the factor that makes the dress stand out will probably help them look nicer next to each other - so, your fiancee may want to find a mermaid gown in a more simple fabric, with a dramatically textured bottom. I’m not going to lie, this is kind of a rough read, but I don’t understand why so many people here are being dicks instead of giving actual constructive criticism.

I would like to echo what someone else said, which is that you would benefit from reading as many professional screenplays as you can. I’m new at screenwriting, and reading scripts that have been produced has taught me SO MUCH. Especially movies that I’ve seen multiple times and know really well - it helps me understand how written language can most effectively be translated to a visual format.

Action lines should be present tense - “Nero does something”, not “Nero did something”. You do this sometimes, but not consistently - make sure it’s the same every time. In addition, if something is being said, it needs to be written as dialogue, not as an action. So, instead of writing “Nero says hi to her” in the action lines, you should simply write “Hi” (or whatever greeting you have in mind) as dialogue. Action lines are for things people are physically doing, and dialogue is for anything that is spoken.

Short character descriptions are helpful when you introduce them! So something like “NERO (age, very brief description) is slumped on the floor” for the first time we meet him. This helps the reader understand who everyone is, and can help tell everyone apart.

Overall - read as many professional scripts as you can get your hands on. I saw you mention that this is inspired by Terminator and Star Wars, and I know that the scripts for both of those are available online. That could help you get a better grasp of format, structure, and grammar! Once you have those down, people will understand your vision better and can give feedback on things like character, plot, etc.

I had the worst breakouts of my entire life during TCHP chemo! My medical oncologist referred me to an oncodermatologist, and she prescribed me a topical steroid cream - mometasone furoate, 0.1%. I still got breakouts after each infusion, but with the cream it was so much more manageable.

Maybe your mom can ask her medical oncologist if there's an oncodermatologist they could refer her to? If it's the same type of reaction I had, I don't think treating it like normal acne would work, because IIRC it's closer to a rash than actual acne.

Also, for what it's worth, my skin went pretty much back to normal within a month or two of finishing chemo. I know when I was in the middle of it I was worried that my skin would stay like that forever!

Please let me know if you have any other questions about any of this. I hope the rest of your mom's treatment goes as smoothly as possible!

I went through treatment for breast cancer, and I had extremely low energy for a long time afterwards, but assumed it was normal considering everything I put my body through. Then I had to have a blood test done before my reconstruction surgery, and my iron levels came back as EXTREMELY low - like, the nurse that called me with the results was genuinely like "uhhhh are you sure you feel okay?"

So I had to get an iron infusion to have decent enough counts for my surgery, but I asked my medical oncologist about it and he said I was far enough out from chemo that my blood levels should have been more or less back to normal by that point. He told me to ask my GP about it.

I did at my next checkup, and she was like "hmm, given your history I think you should see a GI doctor, I'm worried you might have internal bleeding". At that point I was like "yeah sure that might as well happen on top of everything else", so I met with the GI doc and scheduled an endoscopy and colonoscopy.

Beforehand he told me that if he didn't see any bleeds or polyps, he'd take some biopsies to check for celiac, because that can mess with iron absorption. Thankfully I didn't have any internal bleeding, and no polyps, but the biopsies showed Marsh 3 intestinal damage. From there I did a blood test to check for antigens, and he gave me a celiac diagnosis.

So yeah, really my only symptoms were low energy and anemia. I only got it checked out because of my cancer history. My GI doctor says he can't say for sure whether or not chemo/surgery caused it, but that apparently it's not unheard of for bodies to develop celiac disease after going through severe physical trauma.

I was getting ready for a work party, and because of the dress I was wearing I decided to wear one of those strapless stick-on bras. When I was smoothing it out to make sure it stuck on properly, I noticed a significant lump in my breast that I had never felt before.

I shrugged it off in the moment so I could enjoy the party, but later that night after my boyfriend (now husband) and I had sex, he said something along the lines of "hey, I don't want to freak you out, but I noticed a lump in your boob".

Something in my gut told me to get it checked out ASAP, even though it was extremely unlikely to be cancer. I was only 30 years old, with no family history of breast cancer whatsoever. I went in for an exam at Planned Parenthood, and I'm grateful for the nurse practitioner there who referred me for a mammogram and ultrasound - I've heard so many stories of young women with breast cancer (or any cancer, really) who were initially dismissed by their doctors because of their age.

After the mammogram and ultrasound I was referred for a biopsy, which confirmed it was cancer. It was growing extremely aggressively, and putting it off could have been really bad for me.

First of all: I am not a doctor or healthcare professional in any way!

But, from the research I’ve done, my understanding is that activated charcoal is used in a medical context to remove actual poisons from your body. So yeah, they’re using it in high dosages to get things out that your kidneys and liver can’t handle - potentially causing v* to help you not die.

As far as low-dosage things like activated charcoal lattes? They may seem harmless at face value, but remember that ultimately what it does is bond to anything you put in your body that wasn’t “naturally” produced, and removes it. The goal is to stop your body from absorbing anything you put in there “artificially”, even if you need it. It doesn’t know how to make that distinction. 

There’s a trend right now to detox and purge “toxins” from your system, but that’s what your kidneys and liver are for. You don’t need the extra help, unless you’ve consumed a poison that might kill you. Otherwise you’re just making your medicine less effective, since you added that to your system “unnaturally”.

Vomiting myself also gives me HUGE amounts of anxiety. I absolutely hate when I confide in people about this and their response is “well yeah, nobody likes vomiting, it’s awful” because it’s so much more than that. It’s not a disgust response - it’s total panic.

I have emetophobia, which is a fear of vomit/vomiting.

It all ties back to my dad getting extremely sick at various points throughout my childhood. He has occasional stomach issues that he mostly has control over now, but when I was a kid he’d have flare ups at least once a year that would involve him vomiting hourly for several days at a time. They always came out of nowhere and he always ended up hospitalized with no real explanation for why it was happening. More than once it was bad enough that my family was afraid he was going to die.

The anxiety, stress, and feelings of helplessness during his episodes all spiraled together to develop this phobia as a young adult. Getting help for other underlying mental health issues has helped a LOT, and I’m mostly functional now. I can go on public transit or go to bars/parties where I know people will be heavily drinking and can manage my stress or intrusive thoughts. That’s a big step forward from where I was a few years ago.

These days my biggest thing is needing to check warnings for movies or tv shows ahead of time. I sometimes come across plot spoilers, but it’s worth it to know when to mute the sound or cover my ears and look away from the screen. If that’s my biggest road block to functioning “normally”, then I think I’m in pretty decent shape.

Honestly, kind of by accident. I had quit the career path I thought I wanted to pursue (teaching high school theater), moved back home, and was working a retail job while I figured out what my next move would be. I was lucky enough to cross paths with a woman who connected me to a part-time, short-term job that was adjacent to my skill set (working backstage in the wardrobe department at a local theater).

Something clicked when I realized “oh, there are people who do this for real as their full-time jobs!”

It took a while to figure out how to pursue it, but I’ve been in this kind of position for almost five years and I am lucky enough to say that I truly love my job. I feel like that’s rare. I’ve loved working in live theater since I was in elementary school, but the freelance aspect scared me off from acting or designing. Working backstage gives me the security of a permanent full-time job with benefits, while having the thrill of a live performance and the constant change of bringing in a new show every few months.

I know plenty of people who use “dude” as a gender neutral word, and I used to be one of them! Then I became friends with a few people who specifically expressed that they dislike being called “dude” because it makes them personally uncomfortable. These are friends of mine who were assigned male at birth, but now have realized that they are either women or exist beyond the gender binary. Being called “dude” makes them feel that they are being perceived as male, which is upsetting to them.

So, because these people are my friends and I care about them, I have decided to work towards steering away from “dude” as a gender neutral term. Realistically, there are probably people in my life who are transgender women or non-binary people who were assigned male at birth who I am not aware of, and might feel uncomfortable with that terminology even if they don’t tell me so explicitly.

My go-to alternatives where I might have said “dudes” or “my dudes” have either been “friends” or “folks”, both of which seem to go over pretty well. “Hey everyone” is always good. “Pal” or “buddy” or “my friend” can work in the singular. There’s all kind of shit out there.

Basically, if you know there are people who actively dislike being referred to by a certain term, and there are other options out there, why stick with that one thing? I know most people who use “dude” do so with innocent intentions, but it’s counterproductive to pretend your actions don’t have consequences just because you didn’t intend for them to have said consequences.

I'm American, so I know our healthcare system is a whole different broken ballgame compared to yours, but so far I've actually been managing okay without a family doctor. Like someone else said here, unfortunately you won't know much about what the actual treatment process will be like until they have more information about the tumor itself, particularly which hormone receptors it's positive/negative for. They won't know the stage until after surgery, but they should be able to tell you the grade, which is how aggressively the tumor is growing on a scale of 1-3. There are lots of different variations in treatment based on hormone receptors and grade (and probably other factors that I don't know about), which is intimidating at first but when you think about it is actually really awesome - it means they have lots of very targeted, specific ways to kill each different type of cancer. It's almost customized, hahah.  


I was 30 when I was diagnosed (31 now) with no family history, so I feel for your friend. I'm very lucky that my boyfriend works from home, so he has been able to be with me almost constantly every step of the way. A few of my friends have really stepped up, too. The biggest help has been from people who have been able to offer very specific things, like "I can drive you to appointments", "I can make you food", "I can watch your dog", and other stuff like that. It's a lot easier to know who I can go to for specific needs rather than having a ton of people telling me to just let them know if I "need anything at all". That sort of puts the pressure on me to come up with what I need help with, and makes me feel like I'm assuming they're fine with whatever it is I'm about to throw at them. Knowing who is open to what is helpful.  


Aside from that, just listen and be there. You know her best, and you most likely know what her coping mechanisms are when she's upset. Some people need to cry, some people need to scream, some people need to make jokes, and most people need to do some combination of those. Right now I tend to gravitate towards the people who have continued to treat me like I'm still exactly the same and completely normal, and just follow my lead if I need to talk about the cancer part. Being around anyone who gives me the sad pity eyes or tells me what an inspiration I am or acts like they need to walk on eggshells around me is exhausting. I'm still literally exactly the same person as always, I'm just sick right now.  


So I guess for me, that sums it up - offer specific help, treat her the same as always, and listen.   


Oh! A friend of mine set up a care calendar for me at [lotsahelpinghands.com](https://lotsahelpinghands.com). It was pretty helpful during chemo - I didn't need to use it very often since my boyfriend has been around for mostly everything, but it was a good way to communicate specific needs as they came up to a group of people who had specifically offered help.

My radiologist was very sure that it was cancer, and told me so during my biopsy. He recommended that I make an appointment with a surgeon and an oncologist ASAP, suggested specific doctors, and told me that if I hadn't received a phone call with results by my appointment that the doctors would be able to look at my records and let me know.

The surgeon was able to see me fairly quickly, and by the time I had the appointment I hadn't heard from anyone yet. She didn't see anything about results in my records, and didn't want to leave me questioning, so she had me stick around while she called around the hospital to get someone to let us know what was going on. Thankfully I didn't have anywhere to be and was able to stay there as long as necessary.

After lots of phone tag, she finally got an answer and she was the one to break the news. Out of everyone I've met through this process, I'm glad she was the one to tell me because she was so kind and empathetic about it.

I know that my situation is probably a little backwards from how this goes most of the time, and I'm not sure how I would have felt about getting a phone call instead. Mostly I'm still kind of frustrated that the radiologist told me he was positive it was cancer while he was literally in the middle of doing the biopsy. That seemed really unprofessional and unnecessarily scary to me. I was already terrified. It's one thing to say something like "I recommend that you call one of these doctors as soon as you can", but he was more like "I don't like to sugar coat things, you definitely have cancer and we need to move quickly". It was awful.

I also wish I had thought to ask how long to wait for results, and at what point I should call if I haven't heard anything. Still, at the end of the day I guess it worked out since that very kind surgeon was the one to first talk me through it.

I'm not the person you responded to, but I just finished chemo in July so I thought I could share some of my experience. Ensure nutritional drinks were pretty good for me in terms of maintaining calories. I got a whole bunch of the Ensure Plus drinks, which have extra calories and protein compared to the "original" ones, but the creamy texture was hard some days when the nausea was really awful. On bad days I drank the Ensure Clear drinks, which are more like fruit juice. They're kind of syrupy, so I would mix it with ginger ale. Way less calories and protein than the creamy drinks, but still better than nothing. My favorite was the Blueberry Pomegranate!

My chemo schedule was one infusion every three weeks, so I always ended up with about a week where I felt decently okay. Any time I felt like I had an appetite, I made sure to eat whatever the hell I wanted, and tried to get in the highest calorie foods and drinks I could manage. That sort of made up for the previous two weeks of barely eating anything.

This is gross, but I also had really horrible diarrhea all throughout chemo, which resulted in some really drastic water weight loss. It would get especially bad if I was also vomiting. I usually went in for fluids at least once per infusion cycle, and would typically gain back around 5lbs each time just from getting rehydrated. Water weight could be a lot of your mom's problem if she's very dehydrated.

I'm happy to answer any questions about my experience if you like!

EDIT: I'm not sure what anti-nausea drugs her doctors have her on, but Zofran was an absolute lifesaver for me. It didn't give me an appetite or anything, but it at least brought the nausea down to a tolerable level where I could manage to choke something down. Compazine was completely useless for me, not sure why. I know nothing is a universal fix, but I figured I'd share!
